live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card-skimming code planted on online checkout pages
next.in_short: MageCart is a label for web card skimming. Malicious JavaScript on checkout pages copies card details as shoppers type them. Reports describe attacks on retailers, ticketing sites and thousands of small online stores.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro describes Magecart as a piece of malicious JavaScript and says multiple groups are using it.
Malpedia's reference list includes headlines naming Magecart Group 4, Group 8, Group 12 and a group called Keeper.
WIRED reported in 2019 that Magecart hackers were casting the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.
Trend Micro lists retailers, an airline, a ticketing site and online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada among those hit.
ANY.RUN describes one Magecart-style campaign that mostly hit retail e-commerce companies. It says banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
ANY.RUN says that campaign's victims are in at least 12 countries, mostly Spain, France and the United States.

Malwarebytes describes a single line of code injected into a compromised shopping site that loads remote JavaScript. A fake payment frame then overlays the real form, and the stolen card data is sent back in encoded form.
Malwarebytes reports Magecart-linked skimmers hosted on the Heroku cloud platform. It says it earlier documented skimmers served from GitHub and Amazon S3 buckets.

Trend Micro says attackers infect third-party companies that supply code to other sites. They also scan the internet for unsecured servers and write skimming code that works across many payment pages.
One report on Volusion says most Magecart attacks happen when hackers use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.
Sucuri describes the ATMZOW skimmer, which is planted through Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 it used heavy obfuscation and 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
ANY.RUN says another campaign's code hijacks checkout steps, imitates payment pages and sends card data over WebSocket.

RiskIQ reported in September 2018 that Magecart operators registered a lookalike domain on August 13th. It says the skimmer on Newegg's payment page became active around August 14th and was removed on September 18th.
RiskIQ says the Newegg skimmer code is recognizable from the British Airways incident.
WIRED reported in July 2019 that the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months. It named British Airways and Ticketmaster among past hacks.

A report of October 2019 says hackers breached Volusion, a provider of cloud-hosted online stores, and altered a file so that card details were captured. It says more than 6,500 stores were impacted and the number could be higher.
ANY.RUN says a Magecart-style campaign stayed active for at least 24 months, supported by over 100 domains.
Sucuri advises treating unexpected scripts on a site as signs of compromise.
Shop owners should regularly review every script their checkout pages load, including those from outside suppliers.
